utterances.text: Did you know a fair amount about Mr. Zigic's background?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: About Zigic's past? All I knew was his work development, his career.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you still close to Zigic at the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: In 1993 I saw Zigic somewhere around the middle of August, at the marketplace, and then I didn't see him until today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you stopped socialising with Zoran Zigic at that point? If so, could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I didn't stop socialising. That day he was simply taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For what?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I am not able to explain that for you. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When -- I'm sorry. When was he taken into custody, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know the nature of the crime for which he was taken into custody, if in fact it was a crime, or would there have been any other reason he would have been taken into custody, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, according to Rule 90, paragraph (E) of the Rules of Evidence, the cross-examination should be limited to the subject of the examination-in-chief. It seems to me that my learned friend has gone beyond that framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic. We have adopted a slightly more flexible policy; otherwise we'll get involved in a discussion which will have no end. So in any event, we have decided that the main limiting factor will be the time. But it is true that if Ms. Susan Somers starts asking the witness about a football game or something like that, we will stop her, but that is not the case just now. So please proceed, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to just confirm for the record that, of course, as we've indicated, we always follow Rule 90(H), which instructs us to put the case to the witness, so we do try to take that Rule into account when we do our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, we are not going to engage in that discussion. That is your interpretation, but there are other interpretations, as you know. So as not to embark upon that discussion, please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Pursuant to my initial question to you, do you know what it was Mr. Zigic was taken into custody for on that date?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, as far as I heard, there was an accident in an agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: An accident in an agency. And what kind of agency would you be talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: A tourist agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what happened at that tourist agency, if you can tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, a killing occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would the registrar be kind enough to distribute Prosecution's Exhibit 3/244. And if you would be kind enough to put it on the ELMO as well, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Sikic, dated 16 of June, 1993, is a criminal report which was produced by Bogdan Delic of the Public Security Section, as its chief, concerning an incident at a travel agency, involving a death, allegedly caused by Zoran Zigic. The death involved a woman named Danka Petkovic. Is this the incident, perhaps, that you may have been thinking of, a killing at a travel agency involving Zigic in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that case in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know the allegation is that Zigic fired a 7.62-millimetre calibre pistol on the premises of a travel agency, into which a woman, Danka Petkovic, had fled, having been in his presence and having fled from his presence, and by which shot she was killed? Do you know the outcome of this criminal investigation that is evidenced in this report?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know the outcome of the case, because I was not in the presence of Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did it concern you that Zoran Zigic, a man to whom you have entrusted your car, your son, had been brought under such suspicion?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase that. Perhaps I wasn't clear. When you learned about this, did it worry you that this was the man to whom you had entrusted your vehicle and your child?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the incident that the Prosecution is referring to occurred a year after the events in Gomjenica, so the questions being put by the Prosecutor in terms of the time when they occurred are absolutely inappropriate. So that this incident about which the Prosecutor is questioning the witness occurred in 1993, and the event with the witness' son in 1992. We see no purpose to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you wish to respond, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This witness is in Court in the year 2001 to tell us what a good neighbour, what a helpful person and a great guy Zoran Zigic was. I think it would be appropriate for us to factor in on what basis he has arrived at this conclusion, and this incident, if it in fact occurred, occurred in the intervening time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, do you accept this explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike please. Mike please. Mike please. Mike please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence just wishes to underline that this incident occurred a whole year after the events with Zigic's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to repeat what you just said. You can't repeat what you just said. Continue, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you also concerned about an incident, I believe it may have been - I want to make sure it's the correct date - of 20 October -- no, I'm sorry. It probably may have been in connection with the shooting where your son was in the car with Zigic. Did you eventually retrieve your weapon that was in the car with Mr. Zigic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was given back my weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the usher would be kind enough, very quickly, to distribute Prosecutor's 3/245. It would just take a moment to run through this. Thank you. It is from 20 October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In front of you, Mr. Sikic, is a document by a Mr. Majstorovic, dated 20 October 1992, from the Public Security Station in Prijedor, which is returning to you or authorising to you the return of your pistol, which was in your vehicle when the car - I'm sorry - when the pistol was confiscated from Zoran Zigic. It is a Zastava. The pistol is a 7.65-millimetre. Was this, in fact, the weapon that was in the car?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is my personal weapon for which I have a regular license, and it was in the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was this in the car at the time Mr. Zigic was shot on August 19th? Is this the same incident being referred to, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is 765 millimetre pistol, and it was in the glove box in the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was the car also confiscated and returned to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The car was confiscated and returned to me the next day when I came from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was the glove compartment locked or unlocked? Did you keep it in the glove compartment, in a locked glove compartment or unlocked?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: You can't lock the glove compartment in my car. It doesn't have a lock.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How far was the point where the vehicle which contained this weapon and your son was located, how far was that point located from your home? The point of confiscation, the distance from where you live.

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. You mean where they clashed, where the police and the army --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: -- or where the car was?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The point at which Mr. Zigic was shot and stopped in your car, how far is that point from your home?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: About seven or eight kilometres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did your son tell you he apparently had to walk seven or eight kilometres to get home that day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No. The military police brought him home in a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And were you home when he came home?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I told you, I've explained that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was your wife home?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I think she wasn't at home, either, because our neighbour's father had died and she went to tend the funeral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And no one called you from the military police to tell you your son was in a vehicle that had been involved in a shooting; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No one informed me until my commander did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The name of your commander, please, first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Zeljko. I can't recall his surname. He was a Captain Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning to the evening of the 24th of July, you said you had gone to the WC several times. Had you been drinking as well? Did you drink beer or some other alcoholic beverage that night that sent you to the WC several times?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I drank beer, only beer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How much beer did you drink?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you in a pretty good mood?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you managed yourself to carry -- well, let me ask you, how tall are you and what's your weight, please? What was it at that time? Your height and weight at that time.

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: 175 centimetres tall, and maybe I had 70 kilos in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you described the condition of Mr. Zigic as something like all fours. Were you able to carry, you yourself having had a fair amount to drink, able to carry another man you said had a fair amount to drink to the bedroom or to the sofa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my learned friend from the Prosecution is saying things that the witness never said, and especially not that he went on all fours. So could my learned friend rephrase her question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he was not capable of doing it. I remember him saying that. That is what I heard, that he wouldn't be capable of doing that, even. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And so my question to you was, were you able yourself to carry a man whom you describe as being incapable of going on his own to the sofa from the outside area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I assisted Zoran, and this was about midnight, to get into the house. So we didn't understand one another. I assisted Zoran to get into the house. And what you mentioned about going on all fours, when I was asked whether he could leave the house, I said that the only way he could possibly go out was on all fours, and I helped him to get into the house and lie down. I didn't say that he went in on all fours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, he was in such bad condition that you allowed him, you yourself somewhat inebriated, allowed him to take his own pistol out and put it under his pillow; is that right? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he put his pistol under his pillow. I laughed at that saying to myself, "He's so drunk, and yet he's put his pistol under his pillow."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, apparently other people had commented about him and the use of pistols when the noise from Prijedor town was heard, the repeated, non-stop firing was heard, because someone said, "Oh, there goes crazy Zigic again." What did you mean by "again"? Those are your words, "again."

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Whatever happened in town, everyone thought that Zigic was behind it, but it wasn't just Zigic. There were other Zigics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you were at that point a soldier in the VRS; is that correct? That night on the barbecue you were still a mobilised soldier; am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I was still a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, as a soldier, you heard gunfire, repeated gunfire over a long period of time, it appears some perhaps three hours, in the centre of your town. As a soldier, did you think perhaps it might be prudent to check out why there was gunfire in your town?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I was on leave then. It wasn't up to me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you expect to get a phone call from a commander and say, "Check it out," or is not every soldier responsible for his territory?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No one could call me from Prijedor, nor did they need to because my unit was stationed at the Gradac war front.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you telling us that if in this mixed neighbourhood that you said you lived in suddenly someone, perhaps you describe from the enemy camp, burst in and opened fire on your barbecue that night, because you were on leave, you would not respond because you were on leave? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: That would be self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Well, how did you know that it wasn't necessary to defend the town of Prijedor? After all, four hours of repeated, out-of-the-ordinary gunfire would cause someone to think, wouldn't it? Or did you know what was happening, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know what was happening. And regarding the town, there were specially designated units within whose area of responsibility it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were Croats killed in the massacre that night, do you know?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes, because they were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you bother to find out if anyone you knew may have been killed in that massacre, or did you not care, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. None of mine were there, and I didn't inquire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You didn't inquire if anyone you knew was there, or you just didn't inquire period?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I didn't inquire at all. There were some friends and comrades of mine there, and I didn't want to have anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you take part in any of the cleansing operations that occurred in the territory of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which ones, please, date and place?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, and the place is Biscani.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you present in the cleansing of Kozarac? Were you involved of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers, excuse me. To use this word "cleansing," perhaps you should use another term. I apologise for intervening. It's almost a legal conclusion. Perhaps we should limit ourselves to facts at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be happy to if I can find a document in which I believe it is referred to. Excuse me for just a moment, if you would indulge me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For the sake of this question, I will ask you if you were involved in the takeover by the Serbs of the town of Kozarac, and that takeover would involve the rounding up and the removal of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the participation by your good friend and neighbour Zoran Zigic in the intervention platoon of the Centar SUP in --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As it was referred to in a document that I would be happy to have put on the ELMO, but I will not seek it to introduce it. It would help if the usher would please distribute the document dated -- the date is in the first paragraph, 31 May. It is not a signed document, but it does bear a name. Just for identification, to make it easier, it would be Prosecutor's 3/246, and it appears the date may be the one that is referred to in the first paragraph. This is from the Prijedor collection, and it purports to have been composed by, although I do not see a signature, composed by Zoran Zigic, and it may never have been completed. However, it makes reference to a 31 May 1992 participation by Zigic in connection with the intervention platoon, and again, the cleansing of the town is -- of Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is clear from the question of my learned friend that the Prosecution is making conclusions. She herself is not sure whether this is a statement given by the accused, the more so as the text cannot be read, nor is his signature appended. And still less is there evidence that it was compiled by Zigic as alleged by my learned friend. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Because it was found -- it was taken in the Prijedor collection and it purports to have some connection. And again, I'm not seeking to introduce it, I'm asking questions from it. I think that I could get a yes or no answer if I ask for the facts that purport to be contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that was all I wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document states, and I'd like to get your input on it, please: "On 31 May 1992, I participated with the intervention platoon of the Centar SUP in the operation of cleansing the town. The movement of the unit was in the direction of SUP, Sports Hall, JNA Street, Stari Grad," and then it proceeds and discusses a number of events, talking about what was found, found dozens of rifles, pistols, et cetera. And then the second to the last paragraph reads: "I participated in the operations in Hambarine, Kozarusa, Kozarac, Trnopolje, Brdjani, and lastly in Prijedor. I fought and will fight for my town. I cannot deny that there have been some oversights in all of this, but ask you for understanding." My question to you is, did Mr. Zigic ever -- did you know as a soldier that Mr. Zigic may have been involved in these operations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know. We weren't in the same unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What unit were you in again, please, if you could clarify that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: The 5th Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you participate in the takeover of the village of Hambarine in the Brdo area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not take part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had no role at all? If a search were done on records, your name would not appear as one of the soldiers who was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: No, it would not appear; I think, at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You think, at least? You think, at least? You're not sure?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I'm only sure about Biscani, not the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just very briefly, a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: On page 54 of the transcript, line 9, the statement made by the witness was not properly translated, so if I may, I should like to ask the question once again. What we heard, and it entered the transcript, was that the witness had said, "It is customary to first look at the neighbour and then the sun." [Realtime transcript read in error "son"] And in the transcript it says, on page 54, line 9, "First look at [indiscernible] and then the son," s-o-n, and it should be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note, s-u-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: So I should just like that to be put right. And it's wrong again. So could the witness repeat the custom that he quoted, the usual thing that is customary in our parts, what the expression was? Could the witness repeat what he said? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: The rule with us is: First look at your neighbour and then the s-u-n sun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what it said in the transcript is s-o-n. So just a brief intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is s -- the sun, s-u-n, the interpreter's note, and not the son, s-o-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And two brief questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikic, the incident that occurred in the Prijedor agency when Danka Petkovic, the young girl, was killed, do you know what her ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Danka Petkovic, you mean? Petkovic, the surname Petkovic, it's mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And one more question: Do you know whether Zoran Zigic went to prison for that crime?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: I know he went to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After that, did he get out of prison?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did not get out of prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: You mean until he gave himself up to The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Deretic. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have only one question, Mr. Zigic. You told us that on the night of the shootings, when you were at the barbecue, that you took Mr. Zigic in or you helped get him into the kitchen onto the couch around midnight, I think, and I believe you also told us that you and your wife left the barbecue sometime around 3.00 or 3.30, something like that. Now, my question -- and you told us that in between that time you went to the bathroom several times and you could see through a glass or some partition that Mr. Zigic was still lying down on the couch. Is that basically what you've testified to us?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's basically it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have only one question about that, and that is: Could you estimate for us the last time, the time of your last visit to the bathroom in which you looked through and actually saw Mr. Zigic lying on the couch? It's obviously sometime between midnight and 3.30, but just an estimate of what time the last time you actually, with your own eyes, saw him lying on the couch.

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: From between 1.30 to 2.00 a.m., that was the last time I went in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. I myself have a question. You mentioned the shots round about midnight. Was it frequent to have things like that happen, shooting, shots, at around that time of night? Was that customary?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain that and I can't really say, because I wasn't at home very often; I was off with my unit. But that's how it happened that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we say that in times of conflict there was shooting all around, or was it very rare to hear gunshots?

utterances.speaker: IVICA SIKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a regular thing to hear gunshots. Sometimes it was sporadic gunfire, sometimes there was a burst of gunfire, but that night there was a particular amount of shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. We have no further questions for you, Witness. Thank you for coming, once again, and we wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence. I am now going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank you, Your Honours, too, for your proper conduct and being so nice to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings us to our lunch break, so let us adjourn for lunch and resume afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Ms. Susan Somers, may we now hear you on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution wishes to move into evidence its Exhibits 3/244 and 3/245.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of Mr. Zoran Zigic has no objection to the proposal just made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Exhibits 3/244 and 3/245 have been admitted into evidence. Thank you. Mr. Deretic, have we got another witness for this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Zoran Zigic calls its fifth witness, Mr. Nedeljko Muzicka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many witnesses do you have for tomorrow, Mr. Deretic? For this week, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one witness for tomorrow, but, Mr. President, it might take a little longer, at least -- but we hope to get through that witness by the end of the working day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that will be all the witnesses for this week, will it? We'll get through them all? Very well. Good afternoon. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Try and get yourself comfortable. Let me start off by thanking you for coming. You will start off by answering questions put to you by Mr. Deretic. Mr. Deretic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Muzicka, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us your full name and surname, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: My name is Nedeljko Muzicka, Muzicka, Nedeljko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And your mother?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Marija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where and when were you born?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: 21st of October, 1956, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside today?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I live in Prijedor today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I am a Ukrainian by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I am a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly where you did your education?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Prijedor and secondary school in Slovenia to Ljubljana. I worked there for two and a half years, in fact, when I had finished my trades school. And the rest of my life I have lived in Prijedor, that is to say, up until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I work in the AutoTransport company of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muzicka, do you know Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I know him very well. I've known him since early childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Zigic's house is?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's about 300 to 400 metres as the crow flies away from my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Is your family one that has lived in Prijedor for a long time, one of old standing?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, yes. My mother was born where we now have a house, and my father brought the plot of land where we live today, and he came from Maricka, which is not far from Prijedor, but I was born there and that's where I live today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Is your house in the same settlement where the Zigic parents' house is?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same settlement. It's called Cirkin Polje. And that is where Zoran came to live, actually, to my own street. I can't say exactly when he came, but he might have been in fourth or fifth form, primary school, so we spent out childhood years together and then they built a house a little further off from us. But all that is very close by. I said it's about three to four hundred metres away as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muzicka, did Zoran grow up in his parents' family home?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, yes. They used to live as tenants in our own street, but then they built a house of their own. I'm not sure when exactly that was, the exact date, but then Zoran went to live with his parents in the house that they had built.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: So from when Zoran arrived in the settlement where your house was located, were you friends from those early days?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, we were, and as I say, we lived just 50 metres away from each other. That's where they came to live first. And we were all of the same generation. The difference was just two or three years, so that we are tied by generation ties. And mostly they were boys living in that area, so that we would play together and grow up together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: While you were growing up and when you were young men, youngsters, did you spend more time together later on?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes. We spent a lot of time together up until the war, and then we each got married and we had to focus on our families more, and we each went our ways. We had jobs, we had our families, so we saw less of each other then. But up until the war, we were practically -- we were together practically all the time. We would celebrate New Year's Eve together and the 1st of May celebrations, and did other things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: How would you describe Zoran Zigic as a person?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: You would have to live with Zoran for many years to get to know him really well, and when I say that, what I mean is that it would be difficult to actually get to know him in a short space of time. We had some wonderful events and a very good friendship. But from time to time we were all -- we were all -- all of us, both of us, were restless, and restless spirits, and so sometimes we would get into brawls. But this was never on a nationalistic basis, because we were all a mixed population and nobody asked anybody else what nationality they were, what ethnicity they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What was his character like?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, he was a boisterous spirit, a restless spirit, if I can put it that way. I must say that. And he was a happy person. He would give you everything he had and never leave you at loose ends. But under the effects of alcohol - and we all drank when we were young, so we didn't need much to set us going - then he would become a little more aggressive. Because, you know, we're not all the same. We don't all behave the same when we've had something to drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that Zoran drank?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, I don't mean that he was an alcoholic. Zoran wasn't an alcoholic. But there was a youth centre and we would all go to that youth centre and stick around, because there was not much else to do. There weren't any discotheques at that time, so we would go to this youth centre, and we were the main ones there. But Zoran was not an alcoholic, no. But we all did like to try to prove ourselves, to prove our manhood, so we would drink a bit and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran during the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I last saw Zoran when I visited his house, and that might have been in May 1992, sometime thereabouts. I and my kum, Zoran's very good friend, were there. We went to visit Zoran, but we didn't stay long. We had a cup of coffee and perhaps two beers, and then the war set us apart. We were thrown to different corners and I didn't see him after that, and that last meeting was in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether during that time Zoran drank more than usual?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty, but we all drank more, and the war did this to us. We all had more worries, and so probably we all drank more. I know I did, so I can only assume that he did too. But as I say, I didn't actually see him during that period, so I can't say anything with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muzicka, in the settlement where your house is located and the house of Zoran's parents, and Zoran's too, in that locality, what was the national composition of the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: The majority were Serbs, and our particular area, the area where I was born and where my house is and where Zoran's parents' were tenants, where they came to live first, those are people like my mother. They came from Czechoslovakia. We call them Pemci. They were of Czech origin. But in Cirkin Polje there were a small number of Muslims too, but as I say, the majority population were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Were there any Croats?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, as I say, where we lived, they were people of Czech origin. I wouldn't say that they were actually Bosnian Croats. They were Czechs, and their origins and roots were in Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that what their religion was?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes. They were Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nedeljko, after the war broke out in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina in Prijedor municipality, did you feel any changes in Zoran's attitude towards people, especially people of different -- from different ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. In our settlement there was never anything like that, and when I say that, I say that with absolute certainty. He came once and he brought a box of cigarettes to a woman. I didn't see him then, but my parents said that Zoran had been. And if he had done anything to harm anybody, he wouldn't have been able to take one step forward. And probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, Witness, for purposes of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: So he would have had to deal with me if he had done anything amiss, but I don't think that it ever entered his mind to do anything of that kind in the environment where he grew up, and I say that with absolute certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After the beginning of the war, were you mobilised into the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zoran was mobilised?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes. I had heard from my kum that Zoran, too, had been mobilised, but I don't know which unit he was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that you are a Ukrainian by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: What made you respond to the call-up by the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, it was logical, a logical follow-on from the events, because as I've already said, we grew up there without any feelings of extreme nationalism. For example, my wife is a Serb; my brother-in-law is a Serb; my kum is a Serb, and a kum is very important where we come from. And when we received our call-up to mobilise and to go to the war, we all responded because my head isn't worth more than the heads of my neighbours and friends and the people that I had grown up with, so we all went, and I went with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muzicka, do you know when power was taken over in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, we all know that: on the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether during the takeover of power by the Serbs in Prijedor there were any incidents?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no incidents. Just one morning we came to work, and we heard that power had been taken over. There was no shooting. It was -- it happened by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Muslim extremists attacked Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, on the 30th of May, a month later, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The objection is my learned friend is using the word "extremist," performing a conclusion. I object to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand corrected, Mr. President, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go on to my next question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: During the attack on Prijedor, do you know whether there were Serb soldiers who were killed, Serb policemen who were killed, and whether there were casualties on the side of the attackers?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I know that there were killed among those that you mentioned. Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the investigation centres within the territory of Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I know, as everyone else knows in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know when they were formed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty, but it was when the events occurred in Prijedor. I think it was after the attack on Prijedor that these centres started to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Could you list those investigation centres?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes: Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to who was taken to those investigation centres?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, you see, this was after the attack on Prijedor when people, males, were taken into custody; I can't exactly tell you what age. But that is when it started, after the attack on Prijedor, probably due to the participation of certain persons in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone from your neighbourhood was taken to those investigation centres of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do have such knowledge. Maybe the second or third street away from us near the hospital, I think - I can't say with certainty - but two men were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they were taken?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I don't know. I know them well, but I'm not aware of the reasons for their detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Prijedor, as you have just said, you were mobilised, as was Zoran Zigic. Did you see him after that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No. Actually, I have already said that I saw him before the attack on Prijedor. I can't remember the exact date. And after the attack, I didn't see him, and we had already moved on to another front line so that I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did you come on leave?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did go home on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, after spending how much time on the front line would you come home on leave?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: During the first year we had regular shifts, and then later in the company I work in, in which I'm still employed, AutoTransport, I was under work obligation, and then towards the war I was mobilised again. A year prior to the end of the war, there was a shortage of personnel. There were people who were sick, others were killed, and others wounded, so shifts were not so regular because of this shortage of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: So during that time period, I'm referring to the period from the attack on Prijedor until the end of the war, did you ever hear from anyone in your neighbourhood that Zoran Zigic had hurt any one of them in any way, verbally, physically, or treated anyone incorrectly within that time period, and especially on the basis of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. I categorically assert, and I stand by what I say, I would have heard if he had done any such things. And I heard from my parents that he had brought a box of cigarettes to a woman who was related to my mother. And I have already said that I wouldn't take a step to assist him, a single step to assist him if I had heard that he had done anything like that. And I'm quite sure of what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. President, why have you decided to testify before this Tribunal for Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I decided to come because we have many years of friendship behind us, our childhood, many pleasant moments that we shared in our lifetime. And I think that Zoran would assist me, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Would you have testified in his favour if you had heard anything bad about him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I don't have much trust in various rumours and stories until I see for myself, and whatever people say, these are exaggerations; everyone adds a little to those stories. I just want to give you one further example. We were very young at the time, and in this youth centre where we would spend some time, where Zoran used to play, a fight broke out between one of our colleagues and a grown-up. We were much younger than he was. Zoran was not there. When Zoran arrived and when he heard what had happened, without giving it a second thought, he fought this person, who was much stronger than he was. And we all took part, but it was all attributed to Zoran, and these men later caught Zoran and beat him up. What I'm trying to say is that many things that we all took part in were attributed to Zoran, and I think the same applies to the period during the war. Because amongst us he was the loudest. He stood out most. So that from our youthful days, I know many things were attributed to him alone, although all of us took part, all the young guys that were friends with Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Muzicka. Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Deretic. Witness, you are now going to answer questions from the Prosecution. So Mr. Waidyaratne, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, you, in your direct examination, told the Honourable Chamber as to what connection that you had with Mr. Zoran Zigic during your young days. Could you kindly tell the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: -- as to where Mr. Zoran Zigic lived before the war, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I know that Zoran was working in Croatia just before the war, in Pula, and then that from Pula he went to Montenegro. I don't know exactly when he came back from Montenegro, but I think it was just before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So there was, if I may say, some years that you didn't see Mr. Zoran Zigic after your association with him as a child or young person; is that correct? After you all got married, if I may put it that way? He was away from his father's house?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly for how long he worked in Pula, but I don't think it was for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know that he worked in other countries other than Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that he was in Germany working too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know that he also served in or worked in Russia?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I forgot to mention that. Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So there were certain years that you didn't have any contact with him because he was away from Cirkin Polje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: That's not quite correct, because he would come occasionally and we would see each other, but not as frequently as we used to before he went off to Russia and Germany. But we would meet when he came to his home, the home of his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you spoke about -- you gave your date of birth, and how many members do you have in your family? How many brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I have a sister and my mother and father, and I have a wife and two children, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. You had a pet name, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Sepi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Can you spell it or -- Sepi?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why did they call you that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: All we enjoyed most was football, and you may know that there was a well-known football player in Yugoslavia called Dragoslav Sekularac, and we would give each other names according to those players, and his name was Seki. We mispronounced it, and from Seki it became Sepi. And then my kum, his nickname was Pele, after the -- again, the football player.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you knew Mr. Zoran Zigic. Did you know the name of the kum of Mr. Zoran Zigic, what was the name?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You did not know; is that --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Hasan Karabasic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I never asked him, and I wasn't present at Zoran's wedding because I wasn't at home. He got married in 1980, and that summer I was staying with relatives in Slovenia, so I never asked him what his kum was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I was mobilised in 1991, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During 1992, the conflict in Prijedor, where were you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Upon returning from Slavonia, I started working, and before the attack on Prijedor we secured the various parts of town. I was at a checkpoint next to the hospital, at the entrance to the new hospital, and that is also the way that leads into our neighbourhood, our settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you were -- this is, in short, if I say, you were in Prijedor during the conflict; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What function did you perform at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: We just controlled vehicles and persons entering the hospital and our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you armed and were you dressed in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I was in a uniform, and we were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was the weapon that you were armed with?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I had a military weapon, an army weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it an automatic?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, which unit did you belong to when you were at this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I'd rather not talk about that. That is my personal affair. It was a regular military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You are not prepared to say that to this Chamber; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: It's not that I'm not prepared. There's no secrets about that. It was simply a regular military unit, which exists to this day in the barracks, under the name of the same brigade, and we belonged to that brigade, which still exists today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So this is my question: Do you want to go into private session to say the unit that you belonged to, or is it that you are reluctant to say as to what this brigade is or the unit is?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I can tell you. I just don't feel comfortable about saying it in public. I can tell you in private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May, Your Honour, that we go into private session for a very brief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So during the month of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, during the months of May, June, and July, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: That checkpoint was closed shortly afterwards and units were formed, and I was attached to the 1st Battalion, and we had positions in Gornje Puharska near the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in Gornje Puharska you knew there were many Muslims living in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you take part in rounding up them and arresting them?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your function?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I came there later. They were already there. After our checkpoint was closed, the army was already there, and I came there after the attack on Prijedor. We were stationed in the school in Gornje Puharska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So your position is that the people, the non-Serbs in Gornje Puharska were not there at the time when you came into this post in Gornje Puharska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No, no. There were people who returned home after the attack on Prijedor, and we found them there. Some were detained, others not. I don't know. But there were men there, women and children. And then in the meantime, some of them went off to other countries, to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you were in Gornje Puharska, did you participate in any operations, if I may put it direct to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: There weren't any operations there when we got there. There was virtually no operations there, no arrests. We were like a kind of security, protection to the people who were coming back from the camps already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, during this time, I spoke to you about the months of May, June, July, you said that you knew about the camps Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska. Did you know that Mr. Zigic was in any of these camps?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Whatever I did not see with my own eyes, I cannot confirm, nor can I testify about. I can't say whether he was or he was not. As I said, I saw Zoran for the last time was in April, and whatever I didn't see for myself, I don't wish to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So your position is the last time that you saw Mr. Zigic was -- is that the occasion that you, with your kum, went to Mr. Zigic's house and met him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After that, when did you see him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your position that you saw Mr. Zigic today when you came to the Chamber, you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Correct, correct. This is the first time since that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear that Mr. Zigic was seen at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I did hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you -- what did you hear? From whom did you hear these things?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I heard it from my kum who was with me in the same unit distributing food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has explicitly said that he doesn't wish [as interpreted] about things that he didn't see with his own eyes; therefore, any further questions along those lines means pressuring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, after all, we are reasonable people. Come on, now, Mr. Deretic. Mr. Prosecutor, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, what did you hear from your kum? And what is his name, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: My kum's name is Predrag Banovic. And I tell you once again, what I haven't seen I don't wish to talk about. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Predrag Banovic have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes. I've told you already. He was called Pele after the famous football player Pele.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did he have any other nickname other than this football famous Pele?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did. That was the nickname he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was he called Cupo?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No. No question of that. Predrag Banovic, my kum, Pele, and the ones you've mentioned are quite some other guys altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was he doing during the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: We were together at that checkpoint. We were on the same shift, and when our battalion was established, we joined together. I was in the infantry, and he distributed food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Banovic, your kum, tell you that he, too, visited the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No, no. When he would bring the food, I would ask him, "Did you see Zoran? Any news of Zoran?" We asked around, but I never asked my kum whether he went there. I don't think he ever did, because there are lots of surnames -- there's a lot of the same surname. Banovic is a common surname. And I know what you want to ask me, but that's quite another man, the one you're thinking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You're able to read my mind. I will conclude that area. Your kum, Predrag Banovic, didn't have a twin?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: He had a brother, but not a twin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Vuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Vuk.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Luka, I'm sorry, Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you heard stories about Mr. Zigic from your kum. What did he say? What were these stories about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, I keep telling you I don't want to talk about that, and you keep persisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Are you refusing to say as to what you heard about Mr. Zigic, although you said certain things that you have heard about --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: They weren't actually stories because my kum didn't actually know what had gone on. He never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: But I'm now bringing in a man that's got nothing to do with this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: And you keep asking me, you keep wanting me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, what did you hear from your kum? That's my question, about what you heard about Mr. Zigic.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Do I have to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. You're going to answer. Answer, please. Witness, it is not forbidden here to ask witnesses what they heard, what they heard other people say. There is no rule which stipulates that somebody who told -- and if anybody told you otherwise, let me tell you that it's not forbidden to ask witnesses what they heard. So testimony is not only testimony of what you yourself have seen. Do you understand that? So if the Prosecutor or the Defence ask you whether you heard tell about something, you must answer. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No problem, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, there's no problem there. On one occasion when my kum brought the food I said, "Was Zoran around? Have you seen him?" And he said that he had seen him and that he was with Zoran; he had been with Zoran. But where Zoran was, I think he said that he was in Karlicina's unit, but I'm not 100 per cent certain. But where he was and what he was doing -- and he is the warden of a prison, Sikirica. He was very good friends with my kum, good relations with my kum. So Sikirica said that he had seen Zoran, and that he was in Keraterm, but he didn't tell me about anything else because my kum wasn't actually in Keraterm. I don't think he ever went to Keraterm at all, my kum. He didn't go there at all ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but what information are you thinking about now?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: You mean the information with respect to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned that you didn't here tell about the other pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, my kum wasn't with Zoran, nor did he ever go to Keraterm. I sincerely doubt that my kum ever went to Keraterm and that therefore he had any knowledge of what happened in Keraterm. And I stand by what I say. I have no reason to think things up or add things on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witness. Thank you. I apologise, Mr. Waidyaratne. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned about your kum mentioning a person by the name of Sikirica, the warden of the prison. Is it Dusan Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know his real name. I know Sikirica, too, and we would see each other. I know Sikirica. We had some celebrations with the women. But my kum was better friends with Sikirica, but I met Sikirica, too, because I was with my kum on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you at any time, because you were in -- during the conflict you were in Prijedor, did you get to know that Mr. Zoran Zigic was in the Keraterm camp, attached to the Keraterm camp, if I may say?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I was -- that was in April. I was with Zoran in April, and I think he gave me some cigarettes and a litre of some drink to take to my parents. I didn't ask him where he was and what he was doing. I was never inquisitive or curious, so I don't know who his kum was. I never asked him; I'm not inquisitive. But as I say, that was the last time I was with Zoran, and that is absolutely certain. And Zoran can confirm that, bear that out. And well, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. While my colleague is taking a moment to consult his notes, may I caution you of the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. We are fully conscious of the time. Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that only two men were taken from your locality during the conflict to the camps, is that correct, and you don't know the names of these people?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I do know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You do. Could you kindly tell their names, please?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, I can, but I don't really want this to be -- I don't want the public to learn about this, because they were people who were our neighbours too. Now, why they were taken away, I don't want to enter into those reasons, nor do I know why, but I do know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you kindly tell the names in a private session? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I briefly --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall be brief. I have three questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: My first question is the following: Mr. Muzicka, do you know who ok the people from your neighbourhood to the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Did Zoran Zigic have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: I don't know. I was very good friends with those people. We were all good friends with them. And I was surprised when they were taken off. Why they were taken off, I really don't know, nor do I know who took them away, why they were taken away. And when I was with that man recently, our relationships remain the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zoran Zigic in any way was linked up with the taking away of these people?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, as I say, if I knew that Zoran had taken them away, I would tell you, 100 per cent. Quite certainly I would say if I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muzicka, do you perhaps know - before the war you said Zoran worked abroad - whether he was away for a longer period of time or a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, I can't say with certainty how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Was it a month, two months, what?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, it was longer than two months. I can't say with certainty, but it might have been a medium-term period, not long and not short.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Deretic. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just have two small questions for you, Mr. Muzicka. You mentioned that Mr. Zigic would be aggressive after drinking. Did you watch, for instance, sometimes that he would -- how far would his aggression go? Would he use his pistol, for instance, if he carried one?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: No. I don't think he was actually aggressive; it was just that he wasn't the same man as when he was sober. For example, he would protect any of our women, any of the girls, the women, if anybody were to look at them askance or say anything to them. But if he drank a bit, then he would act differently, differently than when he was sober.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And if he drank a lot?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, then all the things we did as young men, it would all end up in a fight. We would have a fight with others, other young people. But once we were married, when we got married, we would take him away when he was drunk. He wasn't afraid of me, but he respected me more and listened to me perhaps more than to others. So when he was a little tipsy, he would listen to me when I would tell him, and when we became more serious and when we were grown men and when we married, he would listen to me even more, and so we didn't have any problems with him even when he was drunk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Muslims attacked Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992. Was that the reason why you think the Muslims were being taken to the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, I can't know for sure whether that was the reason or not, but I think it was the main reason, one of the main reasons why people were detained, because they had taken part in the attack on Prijedor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Because a lot of policemen were killed and lots of people were killed, and there were other casualties and victims. So I think that that was probably the main reason why these people were taken into custody and why they were interrogated and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But were your two neighbours, the two Croats, the [redacted], did they take part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe so. I don't think they did. I don't think they personally took part. Now, why they were taken off, I really cannot say. I don't know. I couldn't really tell you why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, one of them, I think [redacted], was never seen after that. Did you ask about him? Did you try to know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: [redacted] was seen. It was [redacted] who wasn't seen; at least, I didn't see him. And we weren't such close friends either before the war. But when I was with [redacted], well, we went hunting for a time before the war, and I didn't ask him. I felt uncomfortable asking him. I didn't want to talk to him about the war afterwards, nor did he start speaking about the war and what happened to him during the war. We didn't discuss that at all. I felt uncomfortable and he felt uncomfortable discussing it, so we didn't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But at least did you know that he -- did you ask or know that he was in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Who do you mean? Who do you mean? Did I ask who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The cousin, [redacted], whoever came back.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO MUZICKA
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, this is how it was: He was taken off, but I didn't know where, where he was taken off to. And his wife, immediately after the war, came to visit her sister, and I happened to meet her and I asked her about [redacted].I said, "What had happened to [redacted] And then her wife [as interpreted] told me, while she was on a visit to her sister, told she me that [redacted] had been taken to Omarska and then Manjaca - I think that's what she said - and then he was released and that they went to Zagreb, which is where they live today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: One of your questions you were hesitating to answer, and I think you wanted -- you didn't want the public to hear it. [Interpretation] Mr. President, may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that we're in open session. Mr. Muzicka, we have no more questions for you. We thank you for having answered all our questions, and I hope that you were not too pressurised to answer. We should like to thank you for coming and we wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence and back to your work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. May I just say at the end that I hope that with my testimony I have been able to help you, Your Honours. I don't know how far I have been successful. But perhaps I have been able to give you a clearer picture about Zoran, because I said in the beginning that you need many years to know a person properly, to get to know the true personality of Zoran Zigic, and I think that I have helped you in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. You have shown very good will. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to take a moment and explain what the interaction was between the Prosecution and the registry representative. Inadvertently, a couple of names came out during questioning from the bench which were covered by private session, and we just wanted to make sure the redaction would be made, and that was it. Not to be rude or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Madam Registrar, do we need to strike anything from the LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I can clarify it for the registry, there were two names of relatives that the witness had indicated he did not wish to give publicly, and inadvertently in an exchange they came out. That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will locate it in the transcript and have it redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as you know, we will have to do that immediately. Do you wish to come to my office afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It would be two names: on page 97, line 24, and page 98, line 3. We'll provide those. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well, we will see to that immediately within the deadline that the registrar is aware of, but this brings us to the end of today's meeting. We adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.20 when we meet again. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of March, 2001, at 9.20 a.m.
